claim: Sens protein is expressed in two stripes of cells bordering the dorsoventral (DV) boundary of the wing disc.
source: Sens protein is expressed in two stripes of cells bordering the dorsoventral (DV) boundary of the wing disc.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1A showing Sens protein expression pattern.

claim: The pattern of Sens expression refines into a periodic pattern of S-fated cells in the anterior region.
source: The pattern refines into a periodic pattern of S-fated cells in the anterior region, which can be seen as expressing high levels of Sens protein.
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 1A with cells expressing high levels of Sens protein.

claim: The periodic pattern of Sens-expressing cells generates a highly ordered pattern of sensory bristles along the anterior margin of the adult wing.
source: This generates the highly ordered pattern of sensory bristles along the anterior margin of the adult wing.
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 1B displaying the ordered bristle pattern.

claim: Notch-mediated lateral inhibition causes cells to switch to either low stable expression (E fate) or high stable expression (S fate) of Sens.
source: Notch-mediated lateral inhibition causes cells to switch to either low stable expression (E fate) or high stable expression (S fate) of Sens.
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1C showing the cell fate decision process.

claim: Cell-autonomous positive feedback by Sens and non-autonomous feedback by mutual inhibition are key to the lateral inhibition process.
source: Cell-autonomous positive feedback by Sens and non-autonomous feedback by mutual inhibition are key to this process.
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1C showing feedback mechanisms.

claim: Gene expression output is inherently variable due to stochastic synthesis and decay of mRNA and protein molecules.
source: Gene expression output is inherently variable due to stochastic synthesis and decay of mRNA and protein molecules.
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1D showing stochastic fluctuations.

claim: The magnitude of protein fluctuations is determined by the rate constants of individual steps in gene expression.
source: The magnitude of these fluctuations is determined by the rate constants of individual steps (in blue).
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1D showing rate constants.

claim: Stochasticity can be measured by tagging the two alleles of a gene with distinct fluorescent proteins and measuring fluorescence correlation in individual cells.
source: Stochasticity can be measured by tagging the two alleles of a gene with distinct fluorescent proteins and measuring fluorescence correlation in individual cells.
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1E showing the measurement approach.

claim: Cells with greater gene expression stochasticity deviate further from the expected average fluorescence.
source: Cells with greater gene expression stochasticity deviate further from the expected average fluorescence (black line).
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1E showing deviation from average.

claim: A genomic fragment containing sens was N-terminally tagged with either single sfGFP or mCherry tags.
source: A genomic fragment containing sens was N-terminally tagged with either single sfGFP or mCherry tags.
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1F showing the construct design.

claim: The tagged sens constructs were used to rescue sens mutant animals by site-specific insertion into genomic location 22A3.
source: These were used to rescue sens mutant animals by site-specific insertion into genomic location 22A3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in text with reference to supplementary figure showing rescue experiments.

claim: Single-cell mCherry and sfGFP protein numbers were counted by FCS in sfGFP-sens/mCherry sens wing cells.
source: Single-cell mCherry and sfGFP protein numbers counted by FCS in sfGFP-sens/mCherry sens wing cells (see also Figure 1—figure supplements 2–3).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 1G with FCS measurements.

claim: The highest Sens levels measured by FCS were no greater than 250 nM.
source: For both sfGFP and mCherry FCS measurements, the highest Sens levels were no greater than 250 nM (Figure 1G), corresponding to approximately 25 RFU obtained from imaging (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Stated in text with reference to FCS data in Figure 1G.

claim: The conversion factor between RFU and concentration is approximately 1 RFU equivalent to 10 nM.
source: This gives an approximate conversion factor of 1 RFU equivalent to 10 nM.
evidence: Stated in text based on FCS measurements and imaging data.

claim: The average wing disc cell nuclear volume is 23 × 10−15 L.
source: Since the average wing disc cell nuclear volume is 23 × 10−15 L (Papadopoulos et al., 2019), 1 RFU is estimated to correspond to ~138 Sens molecules.
evidence: Stated in text with citation to previous work.

claim: 1 RFU is estimated to correspond to approximately 138 Sens molecules.
source: Since the average wing disc cell nuclear volume is 23 × 10−15 L (Papadopoulos et al., 2019), 1 RFU is estimated to correspond to ~138 Sens molecules.
evidence: Stated in text based on conversion calculations.

claim: Wing disc cells display a broad range of Sens protein molecule numbers.
source: Applying the conversion factor, we observed that wing disc cells displayed a broad range of Sens protein molecule numbers (Figure 2A).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 2A displaying the distribution.

claim: Both sfGFP and mCherry tagged alleles contributed equally to total Sens protein output on average.
source: Although both sfGFP and mCherry tagged alleles contributed equally to total Sens protein output on average (Figure 1G), there were significant intracellular differences between sfGFP-Sens and mCherry-Sens molecule numbers (Figure 2A).
evidence: Stated in text with reference to FCS data in Figure 1G.

claim: There were significant intracellular differences between sfGFP-Sens and mCherry-Sens molecule numbers.
source: Although both sfGFP and mCherry tagged alleles contributed equally to total Sens protein output on average (Figure 1G), there were significant intracellular differences between sfGFP-Sens and mCherry-Sens molecule numbers (Figure 2A).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 2A displaying the variation.

claim: Intracellular differences in protein numbers are due to stochastic gene expression and stochastic processes in the measurement of protein number.
source: This was due to two independent sources of noise: (1) stochastic gene expression, (2) stochastic processes in the measurement of protein number.
evidence: Stated in text as explanation for observed differences.

claim: Measurement noise arises from differential rates of protein folding and turnover, probabilistic photon emission and detection, and image analysis errors.
source: The latter source of noise arises from differential rates of protein folding and turnover, probabilistic photon emission and detection, as well as image analysis errors.
evidence: Stated in text as explanation for measurement noise.

claim: A tandem-tagged sfGFP-mCherry-sens construct was used to estimate measurement noise.
source: To estimate measurement noise, we constructed a third transgene containing both sfGFP and mCherry fused in tandem to the sens ORF (Figure 2B).
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 2B showing the construct.

claim: Any decrease in fluorescence correlation in tandem-tagged cells is attributed to measurement noise.
source: Since sfGFP and mCherry molecule numbers should be perfectly correlated when expressed as a tandem-tagged protein in vivo, we attributed any decrease in fluorescence correlation to measurement noise (Figure 2B).
evidence: Stated in text as the rationale for using tandem tags.

claim: Negligible Fluorescence Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET) was observed between mCherry and sfGFP proteins in tandem-tagged cells.
source: Negligible Fluorescence Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET) was observed between mCherry and sfGFP proteins in tandem-tagged sfGFP-mCherry-sens cells, indicating that stochastic noise was not under-estimated due to FRET interactions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in text with reference to supplementary figure showing FRET measurements.

claim: The Fano factor for Sens expression displayed a complex relationship to protein output, with a minor peak in cells containing fewer than 200 molecules.
source: The Fano factor for Sens expression displayed a complex relationship to protein output, with a minor peak in cells containing fewer than 200 molecules, and then dropping to a level that slowly rose with higher Sens output (Figure 2C).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 2C displaying the Fano factor profile.

claim: A simplified model of gene expression was created where each reaction was treated as a probabilistic event.
source: To understand the origins of this profile, we created a simplified model of gene expression (Figure 3A). Each reaction in the model was treated as a probabilistic event, reflecting the stochastic nature of gene expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C; Paulsson, 2005; Thattai and van Oudenaarden, 2001).
evidence: Stated in text with reference to model figures and citations.

claim: Rate parameters for sens expression in the wing were measured experimentally.
source: Using rate parameters that we measured for sens expression in the wing (Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Figure 3—source data 1), we ran thousands of simulations mimicking protein output from two independent alleles in each virtual cell (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Stated in text with reference to supplementary figures showing measurements.

claim: The simulated Fano factor from a constitutively active promoter model was constant irrespective of protein number.
source: We first considered a model in which the promoter was always active (Figure 3A). The simulated Fano factor was constant irrespective of protein number, consistent with the noise being caused by random birth-death events.
evidence: Stated in text with reference to model in Figure 3A.

claim: The constitutively active promoter model somewhat resembled the Sens profile of Fano factor experimentally observed in cells containing more than 200 molecules of Sens.
source: This somewhat resembled the Sens profile of Fano factor experimentally observed in cells containing more than 200 molecules of Sens (Figure 2C).
evidence: Stated in text comparing model to experimental data.

claim: Loss of miR-9a repression increased Sens protein number an average of 1.8-fold in all cells.
source: Loss of miR-9a repression increased Sens protein number an average of 1.8-fold in all cells (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 4B,C displaying the increase.

claim: Loss of miR-9a regulation increased the Fano factor uniformly across the entire range of Sens protein output.
source: Loss of miR-9a regulation increased the Fano factor uniformly across the entire range of Sens protein output.
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 4D displaying the increase.

claim: The increase in overall Fano factor due to loss of miR-9a regulation was approximately two-fold.
source: The increase in overall Fano factor was approximately two-fold.
evidence: Stated in text based on experimental measurements.

claim: The increase in Fano factor due to loss of miR-9a regulation is consistent with stochastic birth-death processes uniformly contributing to Sens protein noise.
source: This result is consistent with stochastic birth-death processes uniformly contributing to Sens protein noise.
evidence: Stated in text as interpretation of experimental results.

claim: When miR-9 repression was lost, the small peak in Fano factor was strongly enhanced in cells with 300 molecules/cell or less.
source: Strikingly, when miR-9 repression was lost, the small peak in Fano factor was strongly enhanced in cells with 300 molecules/cell or less (Figure 4D).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 4D displaying the enhanced peak.

claim: The existence of the Fano factor peak was not predicted by stochastic birth-death processes alone.
source: The existence of this peak was not predicted by stochastic birth-death processes alone.
evidence: Stated in text as observation from modeling.

claim: When the promoter activation parameter kon was systematically varied, the in-silico Fano factor profile exhibited a peak when protein output was low.
source: When we systematically varied the promoter activation parameter kon, the in-silico Fano factor profile exhibited a peak when protein output was low (Figure 3E).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 3E displaying the simulation results.

claim: Varying the initiation parameter Sm or inactivation parameter koff did not yield a Fano peak when protein output was low.
source: In contrast, varying the initiation parameter Sm or inactivation parameter koff did not yield a Fano peak when protein output was low (Figure 3D,F).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figures 3D and 3F displaying the simulation results.

claim: The noise profile most similar to the experimentally observed profile was the one in which kon varies between cells to generate a range of protein output.
source: The noise profile most similar to the experimentally observed profile was the one in which kon varies between cells to generate a range of protein output.
evidence: Stated in text as conclusion from modeling comparisons.

claim: Transcription of sens at the DV boundary of the wing disc might be regulated by modulating promoter burst frequency via kon.
source: We surmise from these results that transcription of sens at the DV boundary of the wing disc might be regulated by modulating promoter burst frequency via kon.
evidence: Stated in text as inference from modeling results.

claim: Analysis of mRNA expression in the wing disc by single-molecule fluorescence in situ hybridization (smFISH) indicates that burst frequency is modulated for the sens gene.
source: Indeed, analysis of mRNA expression in the wing disc by single-molecule fluorescence in situ hybridization (smFISH) indicates that burst frequency is modulated for the sens gene (Bakker et al., 2020).
evidence: Stated in text with citation to supporting work.

claim: Sens protein noise comes from two distinct sources: transcriptional bursting kinetics and mRNA and protein birth-death processes.
source: Results from the mathematical model suggest that Sens protein noise comes from two distinct sources: (1) transcriptional bursting kinetics, and (2) mRNA and protein birth-death processes.
evidence: Stated in text as conclusion from modeling.

claim: mRNA and protein birth-death processes generate a constant amplitude of protein fluctuations (Fano factor) across the entire spectrum of Sens output.
source: The latter source generates a constant amplitude of protein fluctuations (Fano factor) across the entire spectrum of Sens output.
evidence: Stated in text as conclusion from modeling.

claim: When cells have a low transcription burst frequency, they experience larger fluctuations in mRNA numbers, which transmits to larger protein fluctuations.
source: When cells have a low transcription burst frequency, they experience larger fluctuations in mRNA numbers, which transmits to larger protein fluctuations, and generates the Fano factor peak.
evidence: Stated in text as explanation from modeling.

claim: As promoter activation events become more frequent, they approximate a constitutively active promoter such that RNA-protein birth-death processes dominate the noise.
source: As promoter activation events become more frequent, they approximate a constitutively active promoter such that RNA-protein birth-death processes dominate the noise, and the Fano factor drops to a constant level.
evidence: Stated in text as explanation from modeling.

claim: The sens transgene inserted at 57F5 was comparable to the 22A3 site in its ability to rescue the mutant endogenous sens.
source: The sens transgene inserted at 57F5 was also comparable to the 22A3 site in its ability to rescue the mutant endogenous sens, as well as express Sens protein in a similar pattern at the wing disc DV boundary (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: Stated in text with reference to figures showing rescue and expression.

claim: Median Sens output was modestly higher (30–35%) when expressed from 57F5 compared to 22A3.
source: Median Sens output was modestly higher (30–35%) when expressed from 57F5 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Stated in text with reference to supplementary figure showing measurements.

claim: The distribution of Sens output was not significantly different between 57F5 and 22A3 when normalized to the median value.
source: However, the distribution of Sens output was not significantly different between 57F5 and 22A3 when normalized to the median value (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Stated in text with reference to supplementary figure showing distributions.

claim: sens expression from 57F5 was uniformly higher across the entire spectrum of cells expressing the protein.
source: This result indicates that sens expression from 57F5 was uniformly higher across the entire spectrum of cells expressing the protein.
evidence: Stated in text as interpretation of experimental results.

claim: The Fano factor peak from the 57F5 gene was greatly increased in amplitude and width compared to the peak from the 22A3 gene.
source: Strikingly, the Fano factor peak from the 57F5 gene was greatly increased in amplitude and width, and was maximal in cells with higher levels of Sens protein, compared to the peak from the 22A3 gene.
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 5E displaying the comparison.

claim: The Fano factor peak from 57F5 relaxed to a constant Fano factor in cells with higher Sens output that was indistinguishable from the constant Fano level in 22A3 cells.
source: However, the peak from 57F5 did relax to a constant Fano factor in cells with higher Sens output. This level was indistinguishable from the constant Fano level in 22A3 cells with comparable Sens output (Figure 5E).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 5E displaying the comparison.

claim: The 57F5 alleles do not appear to alter birth-death processes for sens mRNA and protein.
source: Thus, the 57F5 alleles do not appear to alter birth-death processes for sens mRNA and protein but do appear to affect some other process related to stochasticity.
evidence: Stated in text as interpretation of experimental results.

claim: The sens insertion site at 22A3 is in the middle of a large TAD, approximately 50 kb from its 5' and 3' insulators.
source: Using published Hi-C and ChIP-seq data for the Drosophila genome (Stadler et al., 2017), we determined that the sens insertion site at 22A3 is in the middle of a large TAD, ~50 kb from its 5' and 3' insulators (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Stated in text with citation and reference to supplementary figure showing TAD structure.

claim: The sens insertion site at 57F5 is in a small TAD, approximately 1 kb from its 3' insulator.
source: In contrast, the sens insertion site at 57F5 is in a small TAD, ~1 kb from its 3' insulator (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Stated in text with reference to supplementary figure showing TAD structure.

claim: When insulators associate in trans, they facilitate enhancer regulation of promoters on other chromosomes by bringing them into close proximity.
source: In contrast, when insulators associate in trans, they facilitate enhancer regulation of promoters on other chromosomes by bringing them into close proximity (Fujioka et al., 2016; Lim et al., 2018; Piwko et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated in text with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Trans regulatory phenomena, called transvection, appear to be a mode of gene regulation in several species including humans.
source: Such trans regulatory phenomena, called transvection, appear to be a mode of gene regulation in several species including humans (Hark et al., 2000; Liu et al., 2008; Masui et al., 2011; Rassoulzadegan et al., 2002).
evidence: Stated in text with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Homologous chromosomes are extensively paired in somatic cells throughout most life stages in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, homologous chromosomes are extensively paired in somatic cells throughout most life stages (Metz, 1916), leading to physical co-localization of paired alleles in nuclei.
evidence: Stated in text with citation to supporting literature.

claim: When mCherry-sens was placed at 57F5 in trans to a sfGFP-sens allele at 57F5, a sizable fraction of cells expressed higher levels of mCherry-Sens, creating a broader, bimodal distribution.
source: A strikingly different distribution was observed when mCherry-sens was placed at 57F5 in trans to a sfGFP-sens allele at 57F5 (Figure 6A). A sizable fraction of cells expressed higher levels of mCherry-Sens, creating a broader, bimodal distribution.
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 6A displaying the distribution.

claim: The distribution of mCherry-Sens from 57F5/22A3 cells was identical to that of 22A3/22A3 cells.
source: Strikingly, the observed distribution of mCherry-Sens from 57F5/22A3 cells was identical to that of 22A3/22A3 cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 6A displaying the comparison.

claim: sens alleles regulate one another in trans when located at 57F5 but not at 22A3.
source: Thus, even though sens alleles are physically paired at either 22A3 or 57F5, they regulate one another in trans when located at 57F5 but not at 22A3.
evidence: Stated in text as conclusion from experimental results.

claim: The Fano factor from 57F5/22A3 cells resembled that from 22A3/22A3 and not 57F5/57F5 cells.
source: However, the observed Fano factor from 57F5/22A3 cells resembled that from 22A3/22A3 and not 57F5/57F5 cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 6B displaying the comparison.

claim: The enhanced noise in 57F5/57F5 cells is due to trans regulation of sens at 57F5.
source: This result strongly suggests that the enhanced noise is due to trans regulation of sens at 57F5.

claim: A small increase in transcription burst size can capture the effect of changing sens gene location from 22A3 to 57F5 on the Fano factor.
source: When the transcriptional parameters in the model were varied, we found that a small increase in transcription burst size could capture the effect of changing sens gene location from 22A3 to 57F5 on the Fano factor (Figure 6C).

claim: Changing burst size by trans regulation might account for the dramatic effects on Sens protein noise.
source: This suggests that changing burst size by trans regulation might account for the dramatic effects on Sens protein noise.
evidence: Stated in text as interpretation of modeling results.

claim: Cells near the center of Sens-expressing stripes undergo lateral inhibition, and some upregulate Sens to become S cells.
source: Within each stripe, cells near the center undergo lateral inhibition, and consequently, some of these upregulate Sens to become S cells (Alexandre et al., 2014; Troost et al., 2015).

claim: For the 57F5 gene, cells with abnormally high noise were located throughout the stripe, including the center from which S cells are chosen.
source: For the 57F5 gene, cells with abnormally high noise were located throughout the stripe, including the center from which S cells are chosen (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).

claim: For 22A3, cells with the highest noise were located at the edges of each stripe, distant from the central region from which S cells normally emerge.

evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 7B displaying spatial mapping.

claim: The frequency of ectopic bristles was ten-fold higher in 57F5/57F5 adults compared to 22A3/22A3 adults.
source: The frequency was ten-fold higher in 57F5/57F5 adults compared to 22A3/22A3 adults (Figure 7D, Figure 7—source data 1).

claim: An ectopic bristle error was seen in one of three adult wings from 57F5/57F5 animals.

claim: Loss of miR-9a repression did not increase the frequency of patterning errors in adult wings.
source: However, loss of miR-9a repression did not increase the frequency of patterning errors in adult wings (Figure 7E, Figure 7—figure supplement 3, and Figure 7—source data 1).

source: The most parsimonious explanation is that bristle pattern disorder in 57F5/57F5 animals is caused by the greatly enhanced noise in sens gene expression.

claim: For sens, intrinsic noise was not sufficient to transmit disorder to the adult pattern.
source: For sens, as defined by the 19.2 kb region constituting the transgene, this intrinsic noise was not sufficient to transmit disorder to the adult pattern.

source: However, when sens was subject to trans regulation between paired alleles, protein noise was greatly enhanced, which was sufficient to disorder the adult pattern.
